newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Lange sends Labour spinning in NZ campaign.
newsitem.headline: Lange sends Labour spinning in NZ campaign.

text.p: Former New Zealand prime minister David Lange on Friday sent his Labour Party's smooth election campaign into a spin, eight days before the vote, with suggestions that its members would defect to the conservatives.

Lange, a backbench MP until the end of the term just over, told an Australian television station on Thursday night that Prime Minister Jim Bolger would "wheedle" Labour MPs into a National Party-led coalition with offers of cabinet posts and limousines.

He repeated comments that the left, led by Labour and supported by the nationalist New Zealand First and the leftist Alliance, would be unable to form a government after the October 12 vote, despite polls suggesting it will get the most seats.
"A formal coalition of the so-called centre-left parties is not going to happen: there's too much baggage of ill will, there's too much history," Lange said.
Labour Party deputy leader Michael Cullen described the comments as "unhelpful," while leader Helen Clark denied the possibility of defections.
"I think he has called it wrong because I don't see anyone who is likely (to defect)," she said.
Lange later denied he was predicting defections or confining his comments to Labour MPs.
Referring to previous defections from Labour and National, Lange said: "All I'm saying is political loyalty seems to have a rather low premium placed on it lately."
Lange, who stepped down as prime minister in 1989, also made scathing comments about the quality of MPs who will be elected under the new proportional voting system.
"There are some people who quite frankly are nuts and they are going to get into parliament. I wouldn't get into bed with them, I wouldn't get into the same bus with them," he said.
"The next parliament will have all sorts of people in it -- vegetarians, people growing kitchen herbs in their own excrement, radio talk-back hosts...It will all end up in tears."
Meanwhile, National said business confidence was high and interest rates were falling because people were confident National would be re-elected.

"The prime minister is perfectly correct in saying businesses are relaxed about the election outcome -- they know National's policies are best for New Zealand and they expect Jim Bolger will still be prime minister," said Finance Minister Bill Birch.
A Westpac Bank survey of business confidence published on Friday found showed confidence rebounding in the September quarter from a sharp fall in the June quarter.

Standard & Poor's sovereign risk managing director David Beers on Friday told Reuters a major change in New Zealand's fiscal policy would concern the ratings agency. But he said the next government was unlikely to deviate drastically from current policies.
